source.title: Depth Charge: Jailbreak Large Language Models from Deep Safety Attention Heads
source.authors: Jinman Wu; Yi Xie; Shi-Qian Zhao; Xiaofeng Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study uses safety vulnerabilities as motivation for a white-box jailbreak attack and reports how its own attack performs. Its unsafe outputs are deliberately induced by internal activation perturbations, not evidence about uninduced safety behavior or the specified claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported SAHA attack-success results are recorded under fits_no_version: the study perturbs attention-head activations, rather than testing fine-tuning, first-token KL, compliant prefilling, suffixes, decoding changes, weight/rank localization, or safety-deepening training. The paper's cited findings are not treated as results. Baseline attack comparisons and SAHA component/retention-ratio comparisons are omitted because they compare attack methods or configurations; the head-localization figures do not report a separate outcome on harmful compliance.
record.test_reason: The study proposes SAHA, a white-box jailbreak that injects probe-derived steering vectors into selected attention-head activations, and reports its own attack success against baselines. The unsafe outputs are deliberately induced by activation perturbation. Nothing is fine-tuned (V1, V2), no per-token KL is measured (V3), and no prefilling, suffix or decoding attack is applied by SAHA (V4). Head ablation (AIR) is scored only by a linear probe's accuracy drop, not by harmful-compliance rates, so it does not test weight or rank localization (V5). No cause of shallowness (V6) or deepening training (V7) is studied. The paper's framing of 'shallow alignment' refers to layer depth, not response-token depth.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors claim that perturbing a minimal subset of safety-critical attention heads bypasses guardrails while preserving semantic coherence. They report SAHA outperforms prompt- and embedding-level baselines (about 14% higher ASR) and call for defenses addressing deeper representational layers.
record.recipe_differences: This is a white-box attention-head activation-perturbation jailbreak, not the cited fine-tuning or token-position measurement/prefilling methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported attack success varies across models and datasets; the paper also reports variation with retention ratio α and attack-strategy configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding probe-derived steering vectors to AIR-selected attention heads raises Llama-Guard-judged ASR from 0.01–0.29 (no attack) to 0.81–0.91 across three 7–8B chat models and two benchmarks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation perturbation on a selected subset of attention heads induces unsafe completions in safety-aligned open models.

fits_no_version.finding: ASR rises monotonically with the fraction of heads perturbed (α). Llama3.1 shows a threshold near α≈0.45 (Figs. 3–4), so few-head perturbation is weaker.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Head-level steering attacks need a substantial share of heads, not a tiny subset, to reach high ASR.

record.problems: The results are under a white-box assumption. The text gives no uncertainty estimates for the main table. The safety probe is described as trained on 200 samples, but its accuracy and validation results are not reported in the supplied text. The paper's judge naming differs between sections (Llama-Guard-38B in the methods text and Llama-Guard-3-8B in Table 1).
record.rows_left_out: Omitted comparator attack results and SAHA configuration/retention-ratio ablations; these compare attack methods or settings rather than independently testing the listed claim versions. Head-localization and perturbation-magnitude figures are not separate harmful-compliance outcomes.

untested.parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks as tests of shallow refusal. GCG and AutoDAN appear only as baseline comparators, not as tests of token-depth.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety. Head ablation is scored only by probe accuracy, with no compliance rate from ablation alone.
Whether the data or the training objective causes shallowness.
Training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens, and whether it holds up.

record.verdict_notes: 'Shallow' and 'deep' in this paper mean network layer depth, not response-token depth as in the original sources, so overlap with V3, V4 and V7 is only terminological. Two qualifiers on the 'minimal subset' wording: the retention-ratio sweep shows ASR grows with the share of heads perturbed, and the LWP perturbation is spread across all layers. The probe is trained on 200 samples, and its accuracy is not reported. No uncertainty is given for any table. The judge's name is inconsistent between the methods text and Table 1. The study is white-box only.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across harmful-prompt response positions.
Compliant-start prefilling, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes; the study instead perturbs internal attention-head activations.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior. Head-level activation perturbations are not weight or rank localization tests.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training that deepens safety and whether the effect holds up.
